patch.value:
## Problem
This repository has a deep gate stack — coverage, static quality, complexity, contracts snapshot, changelog drift, boundary ratchet, five external analyzers, nightly matrix. Despite that, defects still escape to nightly and to users, and the recurring pattern in the history is a class of defect that escapes, gets fixed at one site, and then escapes again at a second site months later.

## Approach
Make the gate the deliverable, not the fix. Every escape closes with a named gate. Class-level fixes are already the informal norm in this workspace; this makes the norm checkable.

## Precedent in the history
Repeated multi-site classes — path canonicalization asymmetry, POSIX-only assertions in specs, silent-zero filter validation, capability-blind hint rendering — each escaped two or more times before a class-level fix landed. Every one of them would have been caught once by a gate written at first escape.

## Boundary
Not blame attribution. Not a mandatory postmortem document. One structured field and one governance check.
Defect-escape ratchet: every escaped defect must land a gate that would have caught it, tracked as evidence on the fixing item

A defined escape class taxonomy covers at minimum: production defect, nightly regression, scanner finding, and review-caught-late; Items of an escape class carry a structured gate-evidence field naming the gate added or strengthened, or a reviewed no-gate waiver; A governance check reports escaped-defect items closed without gate evidence, mapped to an owning item like every other warning; A periodic report shows escapes per class over time and the gates added, so the ratchet is visible rather than asserted
The pipeline strictly improves: no defect class escapes twice
The pipeline currently improves by intuition. Escapes are fixed, but nothing forces the question of which gate should have caught it, so the same class escapes again in a different file.
Turns every production defect, nightly red, and scanner finding into a permanent, compounding increase in detection capability.
Closing an item that fixes an escaped defect requires naming the gate that now covers it, or recording an explicit no-gate-possible waiver; the ratio is reportable over time.

The workspace already records the raw material — resolution fields, close reasons, linked tests, and history — so the policy can be enforced with the governance surface that exists rather than new infrastructure.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
First worked example recorded 2026-07-31, offered as a concrete calibration case rather than as a change of scope.

This task states the ratchet as policy: every escaped defect must land a gate that would have caught it. What it has lacked is an instance where the policy is checked against history and found to have been violated, which is what makes the ratchet worth building rather than merely agreeing with.

The instance is pm-qtbc, closed with resolution "Fixed pm-mcp main-module detection by realpath-resolving symlinked npm bin argv paths." It is an ideal test case for three reasons.

It genuinely escaped. The defect reached a published artifact and was found by dogfooding, per its dogfood-2026-06-12 tag, not by any gate.

It landed no gate. grep -rn "pm-mcp" over scripts/release/ and .github/workflows/ returns zero matches at HEAD b7651d793, so the entrypoint that shipped dead is still executed by nothing in the pipeline. A regression would ship green today. That absence is now filed as pm-u0oz2k.

It is the hard case for gate design, not the easy one. The failure was a silent exit 0 with no output, reachable only under a symlinked argv[1] - so it is invisible from an in-repo run and invisible to an exit-code or --version probe. A ratchet that only asks "was a test added" would have accepted a unit test that could never have caught this. The requirement the ratchet needs to express is stronger: the gate must fail on a reconstruction of the original defect, which is a negative control rather than a coverage delta.

Two suggestions for this task's acceptance criteria follow from that, both cheap.

First, the ratchet should demand a negative control, not a gate. "A gate exists" is satisfiable by a gate that cannot fail - which is exactly the live condition pm-lpqln4 documents for the bunx probe, where an arbitrary token passes. Confirmed again today: node dist/cli.js ZZZ_NOT_A_COMMAND --version prints the version and exits 0.

Second, the ratchet should apply retroactively to already-closed defects as a bounded backfill, because the population of escaped-and-ungated defects is finite and enumerable from resolution text plus closed_at. Applying it only to future escapes leaves the existing holes permanently unmeasured, and pm-qtbc shows those holes sit on the agent-facing surface rather than in peripheral code.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Worked escape, 2026-08-16, useful as a concrete case for this ratchet's design.

Escape: commit 4454ca930 landed on main with 99.99 percent line, statement and branch coverage and blocked Gates (coverage). Three branches introduced by that commit had no test reaching them: the early return in validateSkillReferenceReachability when a skill ships no references directory, the null-target filter when a SKILL.md link does not resolve to a path, and the non-object export entry in listPublishedCodeExports. Fixed in 816ceb0d3; local exact coverage back to 100/100/100/100 over 506 files and 7,410 tests.

What made it escape is the point for this item. The change carried targeted specs and both of them passed - 17 for the surface snapshot and 22 for the docs gate - and node scripts/run-tests.mjs test passed in full. The coverage gate is the only surface that would have caught it, and it is the one local step a scoped change has no incentive to run because it costs about six minutes where the targeted spec costs seconds.

So the gate that would have caught this already exists; what is missing is that nothing tells a contributor their diff introduced an uncovered branch until CI says so. The cheap form of this ratchet is therefore not a new gate but a diff-scoped coverage check: run coverage over the changed files only and report uncovered lines within the diff, which is seconds rather than minutes and would have named all three branches before the push.

Second-order note for pm-2qqcgl, which owns the fact that run-tests.mjs coverage prints the shortfall and exits 0: in this run the wrapper printed both 'Test execution failed; exact coverage still passed.' and 'Tests passed; exact coverage failed.' followed by 'EXIT:0' in the same output, from different sub-steps, while the final combined verdict was correct. An agent reading that log with a grep can extract either verdict. The final line is the only trustworthy one.
